scope: All 423 Pāli Dhammapada positions, with a visually checked published Tibetan concordance and direct native text checks only for the bounded reader selection.
completeness: A documented lower bound, not an exhaustive Tibetan parallel census. The1883 index omits known counterparts. Unlisted or unresolved positions are not textual absences. Published-reference status establishes a scholar-recorded parallel, not near-identical wording.
method: Rockhill1883 pp217–222 were read against all six page images and transcribed as factual references. Direct Derge checks from the reader dataset override differing index numbers. Sanskrit correspondence flags are never substituted for Tibetan evidence.

sources.title: Udānavarga, Ched du brjod pa’i tshoms, Derge Kangyur Toh 326 (mdo sde, sa), vol 72, ff 209a.1–253a.7
sources.license: Public domain, as declared by the source repository.
sources.attribution: ཆོས་ཀྱི་འབྱུང་གནས། [1721–31], བཀའ་འགྱུར་སྡེ་དགེ་པར་མ།. Etexts from UVA, BDRC OCR, ACIP, and Adarsha combined and further proofread by Esukhia on behalf of Barom Theksum Choling,2012–2018.
sources.edition_note: Based on the Library of Congress Derge Kangyur (BDRC W4CZ5369). The source preserves archaic spellings and carving mistakes. Its README flags potential errors and correction suggestions. No fresh transcription from scans was undertaken here.
sources.translator_attribution: Rin chen mchog with the Indian scholar conventionally identified as Vidyākaraprabhā; revised by dPal brtsegs. The Derge colophon at253a.7 spells the Indian name བིདྱཱ་པྲ་བྷ་ཀ་ར; this spelling is not silently normalized.

verses.note: The Tibetan witness says that mind is swift and ends with a wheel cutting off a head. This is a genuine recensional difference from the Pāli ox-foot simile, not a new translation or a typographical repair.
The Tibetan witness describes mind as swift; the Pāli has manomayā. The shadow comparison is retained.

Related passage only: Tibetan chapter 14.8 shares the contrast between those who do not understand and those who understand, but its wording and the pacification through gentle speech differ substantially. Rockhill does not identify it as Dhammapada 6 in his concordance. It is a provisional partial parallel, not an exact equivalent.
Tibetan orders the faculties, food, sloth, beauty, and desire motifs differently. It has desire (འདོད་ཆགས), rather than the Pāli verse’s Māra, as the assailant. The source order is retained.
Tibetan orders the faculties, food, energy, and beauty motifs differently and names desire rather than Māra. The source order is retained.
Sanskrit and Tibetan arrange the roof similes differently; Sanskrit Uv 31.11 is not a Tibetan verse number. Rockhill numbers the bad-roof/desire stanza 31.12. The Derge spelling ཁོང་སྟེང is retained.

Sanskrit groups the bad-roof similes before the good-roof similes; this Derge Tibetan source pairs them. This is its good-roof/desire counterpart of Sanskrit Uv 31.17. Rockhill’s English sequence lacks this exact good-roof/desire stanza: his 31.14 instead follows the bad-roof/passions stanza. No Rockhill verse number is assigned to this Derge reading.
verses.concordance_warning: Rockhill31.14 differs from the selected Derge good-roof/desire stanza; no Rockhill number is assigned to that native selection.

verses.note: Tibetan chapter 28.33 corresponds to Pāli 15; the Sanskrit comparative edition labels its counterpart Uv 28.34. The order of the clauses is different.
Tibetan chapter 28.35 corresponds to Pāli 16. It describes the deeds as perfectly pure; the related Tibetan chapter 28.39 uses white deeds.

An independently attested Tibetan counterpart: Rockhill 1883 explicitly identifies Tibetan28.37 with Pāli 17. It repeats the here/hereafter/both pattern and speaks of seeing black deeds; it does not reproduce every clause of Pāli 17. No Sanskrit counterpart was supplied by the comparative edition used here.

An independently attested Tibetan counterpart: Rockhill 1883 explicitly identifies Tibetan28.39 with Pāli 18. It speaks of white deeds and repeats the here/hereafter/both pattern, without every clause of Pāli 18. No Sanskrit counterpart was supplied by the comparative edition used here.
The Tibetan recension is four pādas here and is shorter than the six-pāda Pāli stanza. This is a complete Tibetan counterpart, not a modern abridgement.
The Tibetan counterpart ends with exhaustion of the taints, rather than the Pāli wording about abundant happiness. It precedes the lion simile in this Tibetan source; the Sanskrit numbering differs.

verses.note: The four pādas corresponding to Pāli 33 are excerpted. Rockhill groups the two preceding clauses about separation from formations with this verse; the primary text has continuous shad punctuation without modern stanza blocks.

No sufficiently close Tibetan counterpart was located in the bounded comparison. The Mind chapter contains other verses about guarding mind, but they are not substituted for this verse. This is not proof that no parallel exists anywhere in Tibetan literature.
This native Tibetan stanza is Rockhill 31.9. The Sanskrit comparative edition calls the corresponding additional stanza Uv 31.8A. Neither 8A nor the Pāli number is a Tibetan source number.
The Tibetan witness speaks of an untainted and unbound mind, abandonment of good and evil, and absence of fear of bad destinies. Preserve these differences from Pāli 39.
The Tibetan witness uses wisdom as a weapon; the other imagery corresponds at verse level. Its wording is retained without harmonizing it to Pāli.
The Tibetan source is Rockhill 1.36, corresponding to Sanskrit Uv 1.35. It describes an abandoned firebrand in a charnel ground rather than silently adopting the Pāli wording.

Related passage only: the Tibetan witness contrasts monthly thousandfold offerings over a century with faith in the Buddha. Pāli contrasts them with momentary homage to a developed person. The shared sacrifice comparison does not establish an exact verse counterpart; this provisional partial is excluded from secure Tibetan coverage.
The native Tibetan verse has six pādas. Its homage to a person cultivating the self is retained, with no wording added from Pāli.
